newsitem.title: UK: U.K. gasoline price war to continue bleeding in '97.
newsitem.headline: U.K. gasoline price war to continue bleeding in '97.

text.p: The ferocious price war in the U.K. gasoline market will lead to further consolidation in the downstream sector next year and keep British pump prices amongst the lowest in Europe, industry analysts said on Thursday.
"Certainly there will be a continuing process of site (filling station) closures and inevitably that will result in more mergers in the medium term," a consultant at Price Waterhouse said.
"You can drive down the road now and pretty soon drive past three sites -- that's sort of bizarre."
"I think there will be another round of price competition to sort things out," he said. "There is still overcapacity in the market."

But analysts warned that motorists may eventually be punished by the intense competition if it leads to fewer gasoline stations -- estimated at 16,000 at the end of 1995 -- particularly in rural areas.

"The degree of competition in rural areas could be reduced but in the main urban areas with high traffic flow I don't see a chance of price competition having a significant impact (on that occurring)," said Stephen Brooks, a principal consultant at Wood Mackenzie.

Esso's Price Watch campaign, launched in 1995, contributed to up to 2,000 site closures this year and aided downstream mergers like the $5 billion deal between French oil giant Elf Aquitaine, Chevron Corp and Murco Petroleum in November, analysts said.
"It makes absolute sense for companies like those to merge assets...The pressure to achieve those sorts of costs savings are certainly on the other players as well," Brooks said.

Gross margins recovered slightly in the second half of this year as world oil prices rallied to their highest levels since the 1991 Gulf War and margins of 2-3 pence per litre were seen as unsustainable for most operators.

Brooks, author of a recent report on the price war, said margins could end up in the 3-5 pence range in 1997, break-even for major oil company operators but not for smaller operators with sales of 1.7 million litres per year.
"If we have another year as bad as 1996 and margins move back down to the levels of summer, which were unsustainable, then we could get more of a shakeout," Brooks said.
"If they settle down into the 3-5 pence per litre range then I think that will be too low for a lot of smaller service stations to survive," he added.
"The independent sector is really in the firing line in Price Watch."
The supermarket groups and the four top oil company players could grab as much as 85 percent market share by the year 2000, from 66 percent in 1995, Brooks said.

The three pence per litre rise in the U.K. petrol tax on November 26 underlined the tough retail gasoline environment, as the average U.K. unleaded pump price had not reflected the full increase as of last Friday, according to Oil Price Assessments Ltd.
The U.K. pump price before taxes, which account for more than 75 percent of the cost to motorists, is one of the cheapest in Europe. The average unleaded price was 61.3 pence per litre last Friday.
